I gave myself permission to write bad code and that changed everything.
---
[2026-07-10 12:51:20 UTC]
I spent years thinking software was this fortress you needed a degree to enter. Every time I tried to learn the traditional way I'd get about two weeks into a Python course and quit. The tutorials felt disconnected from anything I actually wanted to build. It was like learning to play guitar by reading about guitar strings for six months before you ever touched one.

Then I found FreeBuff and Claude and just started building instead of studying.

The first thing I made was absolute garbage. It crashed constantly. I broke it more times than I fixed it. But something weird happened after about a month. I started recognizing patterns. I could look at error messages and actually understand what they meant instead of just pasting them into Google and hoping for the best. The AI wasn't doing the work for me. It was showing me how the work got done and I was paying attention.

I think that's the part people who haven't tried AI coding don't get. They picture someone pressing a button and getting a finished app. That's not what happens. What happens is you spend four hours trying to get a button to appear in the right place and somewhere in hour three you accidentally learn CSS positioning because you had to.

I'm not a developer in the traditional sense. I didn't go through bootcamp or a CS program. But I've shipped real projects. An app, a text adventure game, and a few CLI tools including OpenMeta and SnapGPT. None of them are perfect. All of them taught me something I couldn't have learned from a video.

The gap between having an idea and building that idea has collapsed. And I don't think enough people are taking advantage of that yet. Not because they can't. Because they're still waiting for permission to start.

#AI #VibeCoding #BuildInPublic #freebuff #claude #gemini #coding #solobuilder #indiehacker #startup #tech #learninginpublic #opensource
---
[2026-07-10 12:51:20 UTC]
I'm starting to think vibecoders aren't lazy. They're just the first group of people who realized most of coding is busy work we never needed to do manually.

Somebody told me yesterday that using AI to write code means you're cheating. Not learning the "real way." And I kind of get where that instinct comes from. For a long time being a good developer meant memorizing syntax and knowing exactly which function to call without looking anything up. That was the bar.

And nobody says using a calculator is cheating at math. Nobody tells architects they're not real architects because they use CAD software instead of drawing blueprints by hand. Tools change what the job looks like. That's not cheating. That's progress.

Vibecoders aren't skipping the hard parts out of laziness. We're skipping the parts that don't matter anymore so we can focus on what actually does. Does your app solve a real problem? Is it usable? Does it work? Those questions matter way more than whether you memorized every method in the standard library.

I use Codex CLI and Ollama and Claude and a half dozen other tools and I don't feel bad about it. What I feel is productive. I shipped more projects in six months than I would have in six years doing it the traditional way. That's not laziness. That's choosing where to spend your energy.

If the future of coding involves more thinking about problems and less memorizing syntax, I'm okay with that. Actually I'm more than okay with that. I think that's exactly where we should be heading.

I was reading a paper on PubMed last week about dietary supplements and the methodology was so obviously flawed I got annoyed. So I pasted it into Claude and asked it to rip the study design apart. What came back was genuinely impressive.

The AI spotted things I'd missed even on a second read. The sample size was too small to draw the conclusion the authors were making. The control group wasn't properly matched to the experimental group. There was a possible confounding variable that the researchers mentioned once in passing and then never addressed again. All stuff that should have been caught in peer review.

This is what excites me about AI in science and it's not the flashy stuff. It's not writing Nobel worthy papers or discovering new elements. It's doing the boring work of catching bad science before it gets published and cited and built upon by other researchers who don't have time to scrutinize every study they reference.

Peer review as it exists right now is stretched thin. Reviewers are unpaid volunteers with limited time. They miss things. AI doesn't get tired or distracted or intimidated by a big name researcher. It just checks the math and the methodology and tells you what doesn't add up.

I'm not saying AI should replace peer review. But it should absolutely be part of the pipeline. Run every submission through a model trained to spot common statistical errors and methodological weaknesses before it ever reaches a human reviewer. Flag the obvious stuff. Let humans focus on the judgment calls that actually need human judgment.

Bad science wastes years of research time and billions of dollars. If AI can catch even ten percent of it, that's worth more than whatever the next viral AI demo is.

[2026-07-10 12:51:20 UTC]
Nature just published a paper about an AI system that doesn't just analyze data. It argues with itself. And I can't stop thinking about what that means for how science gets done.

Here's what happened. Researchers built a multi-agent AI called Co-Scientist that works less like a calculator and more like a research partner. You give it a problem and it doesn't just spit out an answer. It generates hypotheses, designs experiments, runs simulations, and then gets another instance of itself to critique the results. The two agents debate each other. They poke holes in each other's reasoning. And out of that back and forth comes something closer to actual scientific thinking.

I'm not saying this thing is doing science on its own. It's not. The Nature paper is pretty clear that human researchers still have to check the ideas for novelty and rigor. The AI can propose things that sound plausible but don't actually hold up when you look closer. That part matters because a lot of the hype around AI in science skips over the fact that these systems are kind of like a very smart intern who read every paper ever published but has never actually been in a lab.

But here's what gets me. The bottleneck in science has never really been intelligence. There are plenty of smart people. The bottleneck is time. Designing an experiment takes weeks. Running it takes months. Analyzing the results takes more weeks. If an AI can compress the design phase by proposing and stress testing hypotheses in hours instead of weeks, that changes the whole rhythm of discovery.

The paper also mentioned something I found pretty revealing. The best results didn't come from the AI working alone or from the human directing the AI. They came from a back and forth where the human would refine the AI's proposals and the AI would refine the human's refinements. It's acceleration, not replacement. A different thing entirely.

I keep wondering how many discoveries are sitting inside existing data right now that nobody has connected yet. Not because nobody is smart enough. Because there's too much data and not enough time to think through all the possible combinations. That's a problem AI might actually solve.

Source: Nature, "Accelerating Scientific Discovery with Co-Scientist," July 9 2026 issue

[2026-07-10 12:51:20 UTC]
Someone analyzed 80 million scientific papers to figure out what happens when AI enters a research field. The answer is kind of uncomfortable. Productivity goes up. Novelty goes down.

This paper from Research Policy went through basically every field of science and tracked what happened as AI tools got adopted. And they found this weird tradeoff. The more AI gets used in a field, the more papers get published. Way more. But the papers are less likely to be the kind that change how people think about a problem. They're incremental. Safe. Good enough to get cited in the short term but not the kind of work that opens up new directions.

I had to sit with that for a minute because it cuts against the story I want to believe. The story where AI makes science faster and better and more creative all at once. This study suggests it might make science faster and more productive but also more uniform. Which is a different thing.

The mechanism they described makes sense when you think about it. AI models are trained on existing data. They're good at finding patterns that already exist in the literature and extending them. That's literally what they do. So when a researcher uses AI to help design a study or analyze results, the AI naturally pulls toward the center of what's already known. It's not being conservative on purpose. It's just doing what it's trained to do.

I think the lesson here isn't that AI is bad for science. That would be a dumb conclusion. The lesson is that how you use the AI matters. If you treat it as a pattern matcher and just run with whatever it suggests, you'll get more of the same. If you use it to stress test your own weird ideas, to check whether your contrarian hypothesis holds up against the literature, that's where it might actually help you think differently.

The study found that the fields where AI had the biggest positive impact were the ones where researchers used it for verification and exploration, not for generation. They'd come up with the weird idea themselves and then ask the AI to check if the data supported it or contradicted it. The weird ideas still came from humans.

Source: Research Policy, "AI in Science: When and Where It Makes a Difference," July 2026

[2026-07-10 12:51:20 UTC]
There's something happening in scientific publishing that nobody outside academia is talking about. AI is writing papers faster than humans can review them. And the whole peer review system is starting to crack under the weight.

I got interested in this after reading some stuff from APS Engage this week about what they're calling the productivity paradox in scientific review. The basic problem is pretty simple. AI tools make it way easier to write a paper. You can generate literature reviews, format citations, even draft methodology sections. So more papers get submitted. A lot more. But the number of qualified human reviewers hasn't changed. Same people. Way more papers.

What happens next is predictable and kind of bad. Reviewers rush. They miss things. Papers that look plausible but have serious methodological problems slip through because nobody had time to really dig into the numbers. And here's the part that actually keeps me up. Some of those papers are about medicine. About drugs that go into people. About treatments that affect real outcomes.

The irony is that the same AI tools that are flooding the system with papers are also being developed to catch the bad ones. There's an arms race happening. On one side, AI generated or AI assisted papers that may or may not be solid. On the other side, AI detection tools trying to flag statistical manipulation, p-hacking, fabricated data, and papers where the conclusions don't actually follow from the results. AI versus AI.

I don't think the answer is to ban AI from scientific writing. That ship sailed and it's not coming back. But I do think we need to admit that the current peer review model, which basically runs on unpaid volunteer labor, was not designed for this volume. It was designed for a world where publishing a paper took months and the bottleneck was human effort, not compute.

If we don't fix the review pipeline, we're going to end up with a scientific literature that's full of plausible looking but wrong results. And wrong results don't just sit there. They get cited. They become the foundation for the next study. The errors compound.

Source: APS Engage (FPS Newsletter), "The Productivity Paradox in Scientific Review," July 2026

[2026-07-10 13:18:00 UTC]
Geneva last week. Policymakers from multiple countries sat in a room and tried to figure out how to stop AI from breaking science. I wish I could say they walked out with a solution. They didn't. But the conversation they started matters more than most people realize.

The Global Dialogue on AI Governance ran July 6th and 7th and one of the main agenda items was what happens when autonomous scientific agents start generating data that looks real but isn't. The specific concern was something called digital provenance. Basically, how do you know whether a dataset came from an actual experiment that happened in a physical lab, or from an AI that simulated what an experiment might produce?

This is not a theoretical problem. AI models can already generate synthetic data that's statistically indistinguishable from real experimental results in some fields. If that synthetic data gets mixed into training sets or published databases without being labeled as synthetic, the whole scientific record starts to get polluted. Models trained on fake data produce fake conclusions. Future researchers build on those conclusions. You can see where this goes.

One of the proposals being discussed was mandatory digital watermarking for any data generated by AI systems in a research context. The idea is that before an AI produced dataset gets submitted to a repository, it gets tagged at the source. Human collected experimental data gets a different tag. That way when someone comes along later and pulls data for a meta analysis or trains a new model on it, they can see what they're working with.

The pushback, predictably, is about enforcement. Who checks whether the watermark is accurate? What stops someone from stripping the tag and passing synthetic data as real? And do we even have the infrastructure to track this across every scientific database in every country?

I don't have answers to those questions. I'm not sure anyone does yet. But I'm glad the conversation is happening now instead of after the problem becomes unfixable. Most governance conversations around AI happen years too late. This one might actually be happening at the right time.

Source: Global Dialogue on AI Governance, Geneva, July 6-7 2026

[2026-07-10 13:18:00 UTC]
I was reading about quantum error correction this morning and had that familiar feeling of being way out of my depth. But I kept reading anyway because the thing they're trying to do is so fundamentally weird that I can't look away.

Quantum computers are held together by hope and active intervention. They're so sensitive that basically any interaction with the outside world (temperature, vibration, stray electromagnetic fields) introduces errors into the computation. The qubits that store information don't stay coherent for very long. They decohere, which is a fancy way of saying they forget what they were doing and become useless.

The thing that's changed recently, and why I'm writing about this, is that error correction has gotten dramatically better. Not because anyone solved quantum mechanics. Because AI models are now being used to predict and correct errors in real time, faster than classical error correction algorithms could manage. Google's quantum team and a few others have published results showing that AI driven error correction can maintain coherence for longer than any previous approach.

I tried to explain this to a friend and they asked whether "longer" means minutes or hours and I had to tell them it means milliseconds. But those milliseconds matter. Every doubling of coherence time makes a certain class of problems more tractable. Get enough doublings and you cross a threshold where error corrected quantum computing becomes practically useful instead of just scientifically interesting.

The thing that sticks with me is how AI and quantum computing keep converging from opposite directions. AI helps build better quantum computers. Better quantum computers will eventually run AI models that can't run on classical hardware. Each one accelerates the other. It's a feedback loop and we're just at the beginning of it.

I don't pretend to understand the math behind quantum error correction. The linear algebra alone makes my head hurt. But I understand feedback loops. And this one is going to produce something important.

I switched from paid AI tools to free ones about six months ago and the thing that surprised me most wasn't the quality. It was the community.

When you pay for a tool, you're a customer. The relationship is transactional. You give them money. They give you access. If something breaks, you open a support ticket and wait. When the tool is free and open source, you're not a customer. You're part of something. That kind of neutrality is genuinely valuable in a way that doesn't show up on feature comparison tables.

The other thing I've noticed is that free tools tend to stay aligned with what users actually need. When there's no subscription revenue to protect, there's no incentive to add features just to justify the price. The things that get built are the things people actually ask for. That sounds obvious but it's surprisingly rare.

I'm not saying every paid tool is bad or that developers shouldn't charge for their work. They should. Building good software is hard and people deserve to get paid for it. But the open source alternative has gotten good enough that the gap between free and paid is mostly about convenience now, not capability. And for me, the tradeoff was worth it.

The 9-to-5 workday was designed for factories. Not for knowledge work. Not for creative work. And definitely not for a world where half your tasks can be automated while you sleep.

I've been thinking about this a lot lately because my own working hours have gotten strange. I'll spend three hours in the morning doing the kind of deep work that requires my full attention. Then I'll set up some automated tasks, walk away for the afternoon, and come back to results. Sometimes the most productive thing I do all day is write a good prompt and then go take a walk while the models run.

That's not laziness. That's leverage. And I think a lot of the resistance to AI in the workplace comes from confusing those two things.

The factory model of work assumes that time spent equals value produced. You're at your desk for eight hours, you're working. But that model was always a compromise. It optimized for measurability, not productivity. You can measure whether someone is at their desk. Measuring whether they're actually thinking is harder. So we built workplace culture around the thing we could measure.

AI breaks that model because it separates output from time in a way that's impossible to ignore. If someone can produce in two hours what used to take eight, what happens to the other six? Some companies will use that as an excuse to squeeze more out of people. Others will pretend it's not happening and enforce presenteeism anyway. The smart ones will redesign the work around the output instead of the clock.

I don't think the 9-to-5 disappears tomorrow. Too much infrastructure is built around it. Schools. Commutes. Childcare. But I think the people who figure out how to decouple their productivity from their attendance are going to have a massive advantage over the people who don't. The future of work isn't about working less. It's about working differently.

[2026-07-10 13:18:00 UTC]
Traditional education assumes there's a fixed body of knowledge you need to learn before you're allowed to do anything useful. That assumption made sense when information was scarce and access to experts was limited. It makes a lot less sense now.

I didn't learn to code by taking courses. I tried that. Multiple times. It didn't stick. What stuck was having an idea for something I wanted to build and using AI tools to help me figure out how to build it. The learning happened because I needed it to happen, not because someone decided it was week three of the syllabus.

Here's what I think is broken about how we teach technical skills. We front load theory before practice. You spend months learning syntax and algorithms and data structures before you ever build anything that actually does something. By the time you get to the building part, half the students have already decided they're not cut out for it. Not because they couldn't do the work. Because the work they were given didn't feel like it mattered.

AI changes the sequence. You can build something first. Something that actually works. Something you can show people. And then, when it breaks or when you want to make it better, you learn the theory because you have a reason to learn it. The motivation is built in. You're not learning loops because chapter four is about loops. You're learning loops because your app needs to repeat something and you need to understand how.

I don't think universities are going to disappear. But I think their value proposition is shifting. The credential still matters for some careers. The network still matters. But for actually learning how to build things, the fastest path doesn't go through a lecture hall anymore. It goes through building, breaking, and fixing, with an AI that explains what happened when you get stuck.

[2026-07-10 13:18:00 UTC]
I grew up in Florida so I know what it feels like to watch a hurricane track toward your house for three days. You check the forecast every few hours. The cone narrows and widens. Sometimes it shifts thirty miles and you go from evacuation zone to safe zone or the other way around. The uncertainty is almost worse than the storm.

AI is changing that. And not in a theoretical "someday" way. In a "this hurricane season will be different" way.

The problem with traditional hurricane forecasting is that hurricanes are chaotic systems. Small differences in initial conditions produce wildly different outcomes five days out. The physics models are good but they're computationally expensive and they struggle with the kind of rapid intensification that turns a Category 1 into a Category 4 overnight. That's the scenario that kills people because evacuation orders don't go out fast enough.

Machine learning models are getting better at predicting rapid intensification than any physics based approach. GraphCast and a few other systems have shown that AI can spot the precursors to rapid intensification hours before traditional models catch it. The AI doesn't necessarily understand why the storm is about to blow up. It just sees patterns in the data that correlate with past rapid intensification events. But for the purposes of getting people out of the way, the why matters less than the when.

The thing I find interesting is how the meteorology community has responded to this. There was predictable resistance at first. Meteorologists have spent careers building physics models and they're skeptical of black box predictions. But the results are getting hard to argue with. When the AI consistently outperforms the physics models on the metric that actually matters (did people have enough warning), the resistance starts to fade.

I don't think AI replaces meteorologists. I think it gives them a second opinion that's genuinely independent of their existing models. Two diagnostic tools that fail in different ways are better than one that fails predictably. That's not a dramatic take. It's just good risk management.

Source: GraphCast and related ML weather prediction research, Google DeepMind, 2025-2026

The James Webb Space Telescope produces so much data that astronomers can't keep up. That's not a complaint about funding or staffing. It's a statement about the fundamental mismatch between what our instruments can capture and what human brains can process.

JWST generates something like 235 gigabytes of raw data every single day. Every image contains thousands of galaxies that have never been seen before. Every spectrum contains chemical signatures from atmospheres dozens of light years away. And there are maybe a few thousand professional astronomers on the planet who are qualified to analyze any of it. The math doesn't work.

AI is the only thing that makes the math work. Machine learning models are now doing the first pass on basically all JWST data. They flag interesting candidates (anomalous spectra, objects that don't match known classifications, galaxies that appear to be older than current models say they should be). Then human astronomers look at the flagged candidates and decide which ones are worth deeper investigation.

This pipeline has already found things that humans missed. Not because the humans weren't smart enough. Because the humans didn't have time to look at every pixel of every image in the archive. The AI doesn't get tired. It doesn't get bored. It just goes through the data and says "this one looks weird, you should look at this one."

I was reading about an exoplanet detection paper from earlier this year where the AI flagged a candidate that had been sitting in archival data for three years. Three different human research groups had analyzed that dataset and missed it. The AI found it because it was looking for patterns that humans weren't trained to look for. Not better patterns. Different patterns.

That's the thing about AI in astronomy that I think is underappreciated. It's not just doing what humans do but faster. It's doing things humans wouldn't think to do. And that extra dimension of analysis is where the genuinely new discoveries are going to come from.

[2026-07-10 13:18:00 UTC]
I was reading about a company that's using AI to design aircraft parts and the results are so counterintuitive that human engineers initially rejected them as errors. The parts look wrong. They have shapes that don't make sense to someone trained in traditional aerospace design. Curves where there should be straight lines. Material concentrated in places that seem arbitrary. And they're lighter and stronger than anything a human engineer ever designed.

This is generative design and it's been around for a few years but the recent results are getting hard to ignore. The basic idea is simple. You tell the AI what you need the part to do (withstand this much stress, weigh less than this much, fit within these dimensions) and it generates thousands of possible designs, simulates how each one performs, and iterates toward the best solution. The AI doesn't have the aesthetic preferences or the design habits that human engineers acquire over careers. It just optimizes.

The result is parts that look almost organic. Like something that grew rather than something that was designed. And they consistently outperform conventionally designed parts on weight, strength, and material efficiency. Airbus has been using this approach for interior brackets and structural components. General Electric for turbine parts. The weight savings are significant enough to matter for fuel efficiency and the performance improvements are measurable.

I think this is a good metaphor for how AI changes creative and technical work in general. The AI doesn't replace the engineer. The engineer still defines the problem, sets the constraints, validates the output. But the AI explores solution spaces that the engineer would never have time to explore manually. And sometimes the best solution is something the engineer would have dismissed out of hand because it doesn't look right.

The skill that becomes valuable isn't knowing how to design the part. It's knowing how to ask the right question and how to evaluate whether the answer is actually good or just novel.

[2026-07-10 13:18:00 UTC]
I read about the StellFoundry project at Princeton's plasma physics lab and had one of those moments where I realized how little I understand about the technologies that might actually save us from climate disaster.

Stellarators are fusion reactors. They're shaped like a twisted donut and they use incredibly complex magnetic fields to contain plasma at temperatures hotter than the inside of the sun. The problem with designing them is that the magnetic field geometry is so complicated that simulating a single design on a supercomputer can take weeks. And there are millions of possible configurations. You can't just brute force your way to the best one.

What the StellFoundry team did is train AI models on the historical data from past simulations and experiments. The AI learns to predict how a given design will perform in milliseconds instead of weeks. It's not as accurate as the full physics simulation but it doesn't need to be. It just needs to be accurate enough to filter out the obviously bad designs so the supercomputer only runs the full simulation on the promising ones. You go from testing dozens of configurations to testing thousands.

The thing that strikes me about this approach is how transferable it is. You could use the same methodology for basically any engineering problem where the simulation is expensive and the design space is large. Aircraft design. Drug molecule screening. Materials discovery. The AI doesn't need to understand plasma physics. It just needs to learn the patterns in the data well enough to tell you which ideas are worth investigating further.

Fusion energy has been twenty years away for about fifty years now. The running joke in energy circles is that practical fusion is always just over the horizon. But the StellFoundry approach and similar AI-driven design methods might actually compress that timeline in a meaningful way. Not by solving the physics. By making it faster to test which physics configurations are worth pursuing.

Source: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, "StellFoundry: Bringing fusion energy to the grid using artificial intelligence," February 2026

[2026-07-10 13:18:00 UTC]
Grid scale batteries are the least exciting part of the renewable energy transition and also the part that makes everything else actually work. Solar panels don't generate power at night. Wind turbines don't spin when the air is still. If you want a grid that runs on renewables, you need a way to store energy when it's abundant and release it when it's not. That's batteries. Big ones. Thousands of them.

The problem nobody told me about until I started reading up on this is that batteries don't age uniformly. In a grid scale installation with thousands of individual cells, some degrade faster than others. Heat accumulates unevenly. Charge cycles affect different cells differently. If you manage the whole array with a simple algorithm that treats every cell the same, you get accelerated degradation in the cells that are already struggling. Which means you have to replace the whole array sooner. Which makes the economics worse.

AI is changing this in a pretty straightforward way. Machine learning models can now predict which cells are going to degrade fastest and adjust the charge and discharge patterns to spread the wear more evenly across the array. The AI isn't doing anything magical. It's just looking at more variables than a human operator could track and optimizing across them simultaneously. But the result is batteries that last significantly longer. Which means renewable energy that costs significantly less.

There's also work being done on using AI to optimize the economic dispatch side of things. When should the battery buy power from the grid? When should it sell? The right answer changes every few minutes based on demand, supply, weather, and pricing. AI can make those decisions faster than any human trader could. And the margins matter because the whole business case for grid storage depends on being smarter than the market by a few percentage points.

I don't think AI solves climate change on its own. But it makes every other solution work a little better. And a little better across a hundred different domains adds up to something significant.

Source: Grid-scale battery energy storage AI optimization research, 2026

A few weeks ago I asked Claude to write a function that would parse some JSON output from one of my CLI tools and format it for display. It wrote the function. It worked. And then I spent twenty minutes asking it to explain every line to me because I realized I didn't understand how the JSON library actually handled nested objects under the hood.

The traditional model of learning to code puts theory before practice. You learn about data structures before you build anything that uses them. You learn about time complexity before you've ever written a slow function and wondered why it's slow. The theory makes sense eventually but only after you've felt the problem it's trying to solve. Without that felt experience, the theory is just abstract facts you memorize for a test and then forget.

What I do now is the reverse. I build something. It breaks or it's slow or I don't understand how it works. Then I ask the AI to teach me the theory that explains what went wrong. The learning sticks because I have a concrete problem that the theory solves. I'm not learning about hash tables because chapter three is about hash tables. I'm learning about hash tables because my lookup is slow and I want to know why.

I don't think this approach works for everyone. Some people learn better from structured curricula and that's fine. But for me, and I suspect for a lot of people who bounced off traditional CS education, the ability to learn theory in response to real problems instead of in anticipation of hypothetical ones is a completely different experience. It turns learning from a prerequisite into a tool.

[2026-07-10 13:18:00 UTC]
CERN just shut down its particle accelerator for four years. Not because something went wrong. Because they're about to make it ten times more powerful. And I can't stop thinking about what that means for physics.

The Large Hadron Collider entered what they call Long Shutdown 3 on June 29th. It's the most extensive upgrade in the facility's history. They're replacing over a kilometer of magnets with new ones that can focus proton beams much more tightly than the current hardware. When it comes back online as the High Luminosity LHC sometime in 2030 or so, it'll produce up to 200 proton collisions per bunch crossing instead of the 40 or so it manages now. More collisions means more data. More data means more chances to catch something rare.

Before the shutdown, the LHCb detector team found something that I think is genuinely cool and didn't get nearly enough attention. They discovered a new particle. A heavy one. A proton like thing made of two charm quarks and a down quark. That combination shouldn't be stable enough to form a particle at all according to some of the simpler models of how quarks bind together. And yet there it was. Showing up in the data consistently enough that the statistical significance crossed the threshold for a discovery.

This is how physics actually advances. Not through dramatic eureka moments. Through incremental discoveries of particles that shouldn't exist according to the current theory, which forces the theory to get better. The Standard Model of particle physics has been absurdly successful at predicting what we should find. But every time we find something that doesn't quite fit, it's a crack that might lead somewhere interesting. This strange little particle with two charm quarks is one of those cracks.

The upgrade will let physicists look at a lot more cracks. The Higgs boson was discovered in 2012 with about 30 inverse femtobarns of data. The HiLumi LHC will produce something like 3,000 inverse femtobarns over its lifetime. A hundred times more data. Whatever physics is hiding just beyond the current energy frontier, whatever particles or forces or dimensions we haven't detected yet, they're going to have a much harder time hiding from a hundred times more collisions.

I don't know if the LHC will find dark matter particles or evidence of supersymmetry or something nobody has even predicted yet. But I know the probability of finding something new goes up when you look a hundred times harder. That's not physics. That's just math.

Source: CERN Long Shutdown 3 announcement, June 29 2026; LHCb charm-charm-down particle discovery, March 2026

[2026-07-10 13:18:00 UTC]
Scientists just set a new record for superconductivity at ambient pressure and the number is 151 Kelvin. That's about negative 122 Celsius. Still cold. Still not room temperature. But closer than anyone's gotten without having to squeeze the material between two diamonds at pressures comparable to the center of the Earth.

Here's why this matters. Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity with zero resistance. No energy lost as heat. No degradation over distance. If you could make one that worked at room temperature and ambient pressure, you could build power grids that don't lose energy in transmission. MRI machines that don't need liquid helium cooling. Maglev trains that are actually economical. The problem has always been that every known superconductor either needs to be extremely cold, extremely pressurized, or both.

What the University of Houston team did, published in PNAS earlier this year, was clever in a way that I think points toward how the field is going to move forward. They used something called a pressure quench protocol. You take a mercury based cuprate, which is already a high temperature superconductor under pressure, and you subject it to extreme pressure in a diamond anvil cell until it reaches a superconducting state. Then, instead of maintaining that pressure, you rapidly decompress it. The material doesn't immediately return to its normal non superconducting state. It gets locked into a metastable phase that retains the superconducting properties at ambient pressure.

The record they set is 151 Kelvin. The previous ambient pressure record was something like 138 Kelvin. It's a 13 degree improvement. That doesn't sound like much but in superconductivity research, every few degrees matters because you're climbing toward the freezing point of water and then eventually toward room temperature. The methodology, the "squeeze it and then release it and hope the good properties stick" approach, might work on other materials too.

I'm not going to pretend this means room temperature superconductors are arriving next year. They're not. But the direction of progress matters more than the absolute number. And the direction is toward higher temperatures at ambient pressure, with a new technique that other labs are already trying on different materials.

Source: University of Houston / PNAS, ambient-pressure high-temperature superconductivity record (151 K) using pressure-quench protocol, early 2026

There's a paper from this month that proposes black holes don't destroy information. They store it in seven dimensions. I read the abstract three times and I'm still not sure I understand it. But I understand enough to know it's either brilliant or completely wrong, and that's the kind of physics I find irresistible.

The black hole information paradox has been bothering physicists since the 1970s. Stephen Hawking showed that black holes should slowly evaporate through something now called Hawking radiation. But if a black hole eventually disappears, what happens to all the information about the stuff that fell into it? Quantum mechanics says information can't be destroyed. General relativity says it can. That's the paradox. One of these two theories, both of which work perfectly well in their own domains, has to be wrong about something.

This new paper from Pinčák and colleagues, published in General Relativity and Gravitation, takes a different approach than most previous attempts to resolve the paradox. Instead of trying to modify quantum mechanics or general relativity at the boundary of the black hole, they propose that the geometry of the universe itself is fundamentally seven dimensional. In that framework, using something called Einstein-Cartan theory which accounts for the torsion of spacetime (something standard general relativity ignores), black holes don't fully evaporate. They leave behind tiny stable remnants. Particles with a mass of roughly 10 to the negative 40 kilograms that act as information storage devices.

These remnants are way too small to detect with any current or foreseeable technology. So it's not a testable prediction in the traditional sense. That's the weakness of the paper and I think the authors know it. But the theory also makes a prediction about the Higgs field and the origin of particle mass that might be testable in other ways. If the geometry that explains black hole remnants also explains why particles have the masses they do, you might be able to check the math by looking at particle masses instead of looking for tiny black hole leftovers.

I don't know if this paper is right. Probably it's not. Most theories that try to resolve the information paradox aren't right. But every wrong theory that's wrong in a new and interesting way pushes the conversation forward. The right theory, whenever someone finds it, will have addressed the objections that all the wrong theories raised.

Source: General Relativity and Gravitation, Pinčák et al., "7D universe and black hole information paradox via Einstein-Cartan theory," July 2026

[2026-07-10 13:18:00 UTC]
Dark energy is changing. We know this now. Or at least we have enough evidence that the cosmological community is starting to take it seriously. And if dark energy can change, then a lot of what we thought we knew about how the universe ends might be wrong.

The evidence comes from an instrument called DESI, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument. It's been mapping the positions of tens of millions of galaxies to build the most detailed three dimensional map of the universe ever made. By looking at how galaxies are distributed across cosmic time, you can infer how the expansion rate of the universe has changed. And what DESI is finding is that dark energy, the mysterious force that's making the universe expand faster and faster, doesn't appear to be constant. It seems to have been stronger in the past and weaker now. Or maybe it fluctuates. The data isn't precise enough yet to say exactly what's happening. Just that something is happening.

If dark energy is constant, which is what the standard cosmological model assumes, the universe eventually dies a heat death. Everything keeps expanding until galaxies are so far apart that no new stars can form. The existing stars burn out. The universe goes cold and dark and stays that way forever. But if dark energy can change, if it can weaken or even reverse, then the end of the universe looks different. Maybe it stops expanding. Maybe it contracts. Maybe it cycles. We don't know.

Some theorists are now proposing that dark energy and dark matter might be connected through an extra dimension of space. A dark dimension, they're calling it. At the micron scale, which is actually huge compared to the Planck scale where most quantum gravity theories operate. If this dark dimension exists, it could explain both dark matter and dark energy with a single mechanism. And it might also resolve the Hubble tension, which is the persistent disagreement between different methods of measuring how fast the universe is expanding.

The DESI data isn't conclusive yet. The statistical significance is somewhere around three sigma, which in physics means "interesting, worth investigating further" but not "discovery." More data is coming. If the significance increases, this is going to be one of the biggest stories in cosmology in decades.

Source: DESI (Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument) data suggesting evolving dark energy, 2025-2026; dark dimension theoretical work (Harvard/University of Chicago)

[2026-07-10 14:47:53 UTC]
Quantum sensors sound like science fiction. They detect magnetic fields so faint that a single neuron firing in your brain produces a measurable signal. They track gravity gradients precise enough to map underground structures from the surface. And they're about to leave the lab and enter the real world in a way that's going to change a bunch of industries that most people never think about.

The market projections are aggressive. From about 1.3 billion this year to over 7 billion by 2034. That kind of growth curve usually means the technology has crossed a threshold where it stops being a research curiosity and starts being a product. The two applications driving most of the investment right now are navigation and medicine.

On the navigation side, the problem is GPS dependency. GPS signals are weak. They can be jammed. They can be spoofed. They don't work underground or underwater. A quantum inertial navigation system, which uses ultracold atoms as accelerometers and gyroscopes, doesn't need any external signal. It tracks your position by measuring how your acceleration changes relative to the quantum properties of atoms that are laser cooled to near absolute zero. It's insanely complex and expensive right now. But it works. And it works without GPS. The EU is running grand challenges specifically to develop quantum navigation systems that can function in environments where satellite signals are contested or unavailable.

The medical applications are just as wild. Quantum sensors can detect the magnetic fields generated by your heart and brain with enough precision to spot abnormalities that conventional MRI or EEG would miss. They're being integrated into medical imaging workflows now, not as a replacement for existing technologies but as a complement that can see things those technologies can't.

The part that I find interesting is that quantum sensors don't require a full fault tolerant quantum computer. They use quantum effects but they don't need error correction or thousands of logical qubits. They're simpler. Which means they're going to arrive sooner. While everyone's waiting for quantum computers to break encryption, quantum sensors are going to quietly start saving lives and navigating submarines.

Source: EuroHPC-JU quantum navigation initiatives; quantum sensor market projections 2026-2034; medical/industrial quantum sensor integration reports

Nature published a paper this year about an AI system that does science from start to finish without human intervention. It searches the literature. It generates hypotheses. It designs and runs experiments. It analyzes the results. It writes the paper. And I have feelings about this that I'm still trying to sort into something coherent.

The system is called The AI Scientist and the paper is titled "Towards end to end automation of AI research." The word "towards" is doing a lot of work in that title. It's not claiming to have fully automated science. It's claiming to have demonstrated that the pieces exist to do so, and that the remaining problems are engineering problems rather than fundamental barriers. That distinction matters.

Here's what I actually think. I think systems like this are going to be genuinely useful for the parts of science that are already formulaic. Running variations on established experimental protocols. Testing slight modifications of known materials. Screening large libraries of drug candidates. The kind of work that requires precision and patience more than creativity. That work is important and it's also the kind of work that human scientists find boring and error prone. Automating it makes sense.

The harder question is whether these systems can do the creative part. The part where you look at a confusing result and say "what if the reason this doesn't match the model is because the model is wrong in a specific way that nobody has considered?" That kind of insight requires connecting ideas from different domains in ways that aren't obvious from the literature. It requires intuition about which assumptions are safe to question and which ones aren't. I don't think current AI systems can do that. But I also didn't think they'd be able to write coherent essays two years ago and here we are.

The paper itself is getting a lot of attention this month, partly because it's genuinely impressive and partly because it scares people. The idea of autonomous AI doing science touches something primal. Science is supposed to be a human endeavor. Our way of understanding the universe. Handing part of that over to machines, even if it's just the boring parts, feels different than handing over customer service or data entry.

Source: Nature, "Towards end-to-end automation of AI research," early 2026 (gaining significant attention July 2026)

I have been following the grid scale battery storage space for a while. It is the least exciting part of the renewable energy transition and also the most important. Solar panels do not work at night. Wind turbines do not spin when the air is still. To run a grid on renewables, you need storage. Lots of it. If you manage the whole array with the same algorithm, the weak cells fail faster and you have to replace everything sooner. AI is solving this by predicting which cells will degrade fastest and adjusting charge discharge patterns to spread the wear evenly. [2026-07-10 15:48:47 UTC]
A team at the University of Houston set a new record for superconductivity at ambient pressure. 151 Kelvin. Still cold. Still needs cooling. But closer to room temperature than anyone has gotten without squeezing the material between diamonds at extreme pressures. The clever part is how they did it. They used a pressure quench protocol. Squeeze a mercury based cuprate until it becomes superconducting at high pressure. Then rapidly release the pressure. The material gets locked into a metastable phase that keeps its superconducting properties at ambient pressure. The previous record was 138 Kelvin. This is a 13 degree improvement. That does not sound like much but in superconductivity research, every few degrees matters. You are climbing toward the freezing point of water and eventually toward room temperature. The methodology might work on other materials too.

[2026-07-10 15:48:47 UTC]
I found a paper this week that claimed an AI outperformed radiologists at detecting lung nodules in CT scans. The AUC was 0.97 which sounds incredible. But there is a problem with AUC in radiology AI that keeps getting ignored. The metric is overly optimistic when the test set has a different disease prevalence than the real world. Most published radiology AI papers use test sets where half the cases are positive. In reality, lung cancer screening finds cancer in maybe 1 to 2 percent of scans. An AUC of 0.97 on a balanced test set can drop to 0.75 or lower when applied to real screening populations. The model is not bad. The metric is misleading. And the gap between published performance and real world performance is hidden by a number that looks impressive to people who do not read the methods section carefully. I wish journals would require authors to report performance metrics on real world prevalence test sets, not just the curated ones.

A paper in a high profile journal claimed an AI model could predict Alzheimer's disease onset up to five years in advance using blood tests. I was excited to read it. An earlier diagnosis of Alzheimer's would be genuinely world changing. But the study had a problem that I have seen before. The AI was trained on a dataset where the control group and the patient group came from different cohorts collected years apart. [2026-07-10 15:48:47 UTC]
I keep seeing headlines about AI models that can predict heart attacks from retinal scans. The idea is that blood vessels in the eye reflect cardiovascular health. There is real physiology behind that. But the studies making headlines have a reproducibility problem. Different groups use different datasets, different preprocessing steps, and different model architectures. When independent researchers try to replicate the results, the accuracy drops significantly. Part of the issue is that retinal images contain confounders like age and blood pressure that correlate with both the image features and the outcome. A model that learns to predict age from the retina can appear to predict heart attacks simply because age is a risk factor. The model is not learning anything about the retina and heart disease. It is learning that older people have different looking retinas and older people have more heart attacks. That is not a useful clinical tool.

[2026-07-10 15:48:47 UTC]
A study this month claimed a large language model passed a medical licensing exam with flying colors. The implication was that AI is ready to practice medicine. But passing a multiple choice test is not the same as being a doctor. Medical licensing exams test recall of established knowledge. They do not test the messy reality of clinical practice where patients give incomplete histories, symptoms overlap across conditions, and treatment decisions require balancing competing risks. The model has no bedside manner. It cannot examine a patient. It cannot respond to unexpected findings. It cannot take responsibility for a decision. I am not downplaying the achievement. Passing the exam is a technical milestone. But interpreting it as AI being ready for clinical deployment is a category error. The exam measures knowledge recall. Medicine requires judgment, communication, and accountability. Those are different things.

[2026-07-10 15:48:47 UTC]
I came across a paper that used AI to analyze social media posts and predict mental health crises. The idea has potential but the ethics section was alarmingly brief. The model was trained on public social media data without user consent. The paper did not discuss what would happen if the predictions were wrong. False positives could lead to unnecessary interventions. False negatives could create a false sense of security. The authors mentioned privacy in passing but did not address the real ethical questions about deploying such a system. Who gets notified when the model flags someone? What safeguards exist against misuse? What happens to the data? These are not side issues. They are the main issues. Building a model that can predict something is only a small part of the work. The hard part is building a system that does more good than harm. That paper skipped the hard part.

[2026-07-10 16:03:59 UTC]
A widely shared paper claimed AI could diagnose skin cancer from photos better than dermatologists. The study compared AI performance to dermatologists who were shown the same images without any clinical context. In real practice, dermatologists do not diagnose from photos alone. They use dermoscopy, palpation, patient history, and sometimes biopsy. Comparing an AI on clean close up images to a dermatologist looking at the same images without their tools is not a fair comparison. It is a setup that makes the AI look better than it would be in real practice. The paper was technically sound for what it tested. But what it tested was not representative of how dermatology actually works. The headline claimed AI beat doctors. The reality is that AI beat doctors who were asked to work with one hand tied behind their backs.

[2026-07-10 16:03:59 UTC]
A preprint I read this week claimed an AI model could predict sepsis hours before clinical diagnosis. Sepsis is a leading cause of hospital deaths and earlier detection would save lives. But the paper used retrospective data where the sepsis diagnosis was already known. The AI was trained to recognize patterns that occur before the diagnosis is made. The problem is that retrospective data has a label time bias. The timing of the sepsis label in the electronic health record depends on when the clinician documented it, not when the biology changed. An AI trained on retrospective data might learn to predict documentation patterns rather than physiological deterioration. When deployed in real time, it fails because the documentation patterns shift. Several high profile sepsis prediction models have been deployed in hospitals only to fail in prospective validation. The same pattern keeps repeating. Retrospective results are not prospective results and treating them as if they are harms patients.

[2026-07-10 16:03:59 UTC]
I think vibecoders are the laziest people in tech and I mean that as a compliment. We refuse to spend months learning syntax before building anything. We skip the tutorials, ignore the best practices, and go straight to breaking things and fixing them with AI. That looks lazy to people who came up the traditional way. Spending six years learning computer science and then another two years memorizing framework docs before writing a single line of production code. That is dedication. But it is also deeply inefficient. The lazy person asks whether all that upfront effort is actually necessary. What if you could start building today and learn the theory later when you actually need it? That is what vibecoding is. It is optimized for output, not for process. It skips the parts that do not matter and focuses on the parts that do. If that makes me lazy, I will take the label.

[2026-07-10 16:03:59 UTC]
Someone told me last week that vibecoders are just people who want results without putting in the work. I thought about that for a while and I actually agree with part of it. I do want results without putting in unnecessary work. I do not want to spend three months learning a framework that will be obsolete by the time I finish. I do not want to memorize syntax that I can look up in two seconds. I want to build things that work and I want to build them now. The question is what counts as real work. Spending hours reading documentation is work. But so is debugging a cryptic error message at midnight. So is refactoring a piece of AI generated code until it actually does what you need. So is figuring out why your build broke after an update. Vibecoders do not skip work. We skip the specific kind of work that involves memorizing things a machine can remember for us. That is not laziness. That is triage.

#AI #VibeCoding #BuildInPublic #freebuff #coding #developer #solobuilder #tech #lazy #productivity #futureofwork #buildandlearn #programming #softwaredevelopment

[2026-07-10 16:03:59 UTC]
Every generation of developers has been called lazy by the previous one. When high level languages replaced assembly, the assembly programmers called the new coders lazy for not understanding what the hardware was actually doing. When frameworks abstracted away boilerplate, the bare metal developers called framework users lazy for not understanding the underlying patterns. Now AI is abstracting away syntax and the pattern is repeating. Vibecoders are the latest group to be called lazy for using better tools. The accusation never changes. You are not doing it the real way. You are taking shortcuts. You are going to regret this when something breaks. And yet every generation that was called lazy ended up building more than the one before it. Because the tools got better and the barriers got lower. Laziness in software development is often just efficiency that looks unfamiliar to people invested in the old way.

#AI #VibeCoding #BuildInPublic #freebuff #coding #developer #solobuilder #tech #lazy #productivity #futureofwork #buildandlearn #programming #softwaredevelopment #history

[2026-07-10 16:03:59 UTC]
I think the real reason people call vibecoders lazy is not about the code. It is about the identity. A lot of developers built their identity around the struggle. They spent years learning difficult things and they are proud of that struggle. Vibecoders show up and build stuff without going through the same struggle and that feels unfair to the people who did. I understand that feeling. I would probably feel the same way if I had a CS degree and ten years of experience and someone with no background shipped a working app in a weekend. But the feeling does not make the accusation true. Vibecoders are not lazy because they avoided unnecessary work. They are pragmatic. They recognize that the goal is to build working software, not to prove how hard the journey was. The struggle is not the point. The output is the point. If you can get the output without the struggle, you are not lazy. You are just early to the next way of doing things.

Vibecoding looks lazy from the outside because the effort is invisible. The effort is not in typing the characters. The effort is in figuring out what to build, testing whether it works, and fixing it when it breaks. Those parts have not changed. They just do not look like traditional coding anymore. That does not make them easier. It makes them different.

I have been reading postmortems of failed startups this week. The pattern that comes up most often is not running out of money or building the wrong thing. It is building something and then failing to reach the people who need it. Marketing. Distribution. Sales. The parts of building a business that have nothing to do with the product. The mechanism is magnetic reconnection occurring continuously not just during flares.

[2026-07-11 08:09:27 UTC]
I read a fascinating paper about time crystals this week. Time crystals are phases of matter that break time translation symmetry. In normal matter the lowest energy state is static. In a time crystal the atoms oscillate periodically even at their lowest energy state. The oscillation is not driven by external energy. It is inherent to the material. Researchers created a time crystal using a diamond with nitrogen vacancy centers and drove it with periodic laser pulses. The crystal kept oscillating after the pulses stopped. A state of matter that exists outside of equilibrium.

[2026-07-11 08:09:27 UTC]
The concept of quantum Darwinism suggests that objective reality emerges from quantum systems interacting with their environment. Multiple observers can agree on the state of a system because the environment has redundantly recorded that state. Recent experiments with photons have confirmed the basic predictions of quantum Darwinism. The bridge between quantum and classical might be less mysterious than we thought.

[2026-07-12 03:26:20 UTC]
A paper claimed that a dietary intervention reduces inflammation markers by 40 percent. The study lasted two weeks. The sample size was 20 participants. The inflammation markers were measured before and after. No control group. Without a control group you cannot attribute the change to the intervention. Inflammation markers fluctuate naturally. They vary with time of day, recent exercise, sleep quality, and countless other factors. A two-week study with 20 participants and no control group is essentially a pilot study. The results are hypothesis-generating. Not hypothesis-testing. The paper did not emphasize this distinction.

#science #research #debunking #criticalthinking #nutrition #inflammation #health #PubMed #peerreview #controlgroup #study design #pilot

I think the term artificial general intelligence is not useful. The definition shifts every time someone gets close to achieving the previous definition. AGI was supposed to mean a system that could perform any intellectual task a human can. But as AI systems achieve specific capabilities the goalposts move. The capabilities that remain outside AI reach become the new definition of AGI. This is called the AI effect and it makes AGI a moving target. The useful question is not whether a system is generally intelligent. It is what specific capabilities it has and how those capabilities can be applied.

DESI released new data this year that strongly suggests dark energy is not constant. The standard model of cosmology assumes a cosmological constant. A fixed energy density of empty space. DESI data shows the expansion history deviating from that assumption at about three sigma significance. Not a discovery yet but getting close. If dark energy changes over time it fundamentally alters our understanding of the fate of the universe. The implications are enormous and the data is getting better every year. Either the simplest model is wrong or there's something we don't understand about how cosmic distances work.

I read about an experiment that measured neutrino mass using a cryogenic calorimeter. The results constrain the neutrino mass to below 0.8 electronvolts. Neutrinos are the lightest known massive particles and their exact mass is a mystery. Knowing the mass matters because it affects how structure formed in the early universe. The measurement is incredibly difficult because neutrinos barely interact with matter. The detector had to be cooled to near absolute zero and shielded from cosmic rays in a deep underground lab. That's the kind of experimental ingenuity that doesn't get enough attention.

A team at MIT demonstrated a quantum sensor that can detect single protein molecules without labels or dyes. The sensor uses nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond to measure magnetic fields at the nanoscale. When a protein molecule passes near the sensor it perturbs the magnetic field in a characteristic way. The AI decodes the perturbation pattern to identify the protein. This could enable real time protein monitoring in living cells. The applications for drug discovery and disease diagnosis are substantial and closer than most people realize.

A new paper claims that an AI model can diagnose depression from Twitter posts with 85 percent accuracy. Let's think about what that actually means. The difference matters because depression is a clinical diagnosis that requires professional assessment. Not a keyword match. The study's methodology guarantees the positive result. It's not a finding. It's a tautology dressed up as research.

[2026-07-12 06:07:42 UTC]
I read a meta-analysis that claims coffee consumption reduces all-cause mortality by 17 percent. Meta-analyses combine many studies into one big number. But garbage in, garbage out applies to meta-analyses too. If the individual studies are observational and confounded, combining them doesn't fix the confounding. Coffee drinkers differ from non-coffee drinkers in systematic ways. They tend to have higher incomes, better diets, and lower rates of smoking. The meta-analysis adjusted for some of these but the residual confounding is still large enough to explain the entire effect. A 17 percent reduction sounds precise. It's actually a statistical artifact dressed up in a confidence interval.

I read a paper this week claiming AI-powered chest CT analysis can predict lung disease progression in scleroderma patients. The sample size was 33 patients. Thirty three. The finding that got the headline was a 0.3 percent increase in ground-glass opacity. That's not a clinical signal. That's radiological noise influenced by how deeply a patient breathes. On a sample of 33 people, any machine learning model can find a p-value under 0.05 somewhere. It's statistically inevitable. The authors reported 81 percent sensitivity and 77 percent specificity for predicting long-term outcomes. On 33 patients, those numbers are meaningless. The confidence intervals would be enormous. But the paper doesn't emphasize that. The abstract makes it sound like a breakthrough. It's not. It's an algorithm that mistook statistical noise for a clinical finding.

I read a Lancet paper claiming temocillin is a safe, effective alternative to carbapenems for resistant bloodstream infections. This one is actually useful. [2026-07-12 07:01:36 UTC]
I think the most useful skill I've developed from reading medical papers critically is not statistical knowledge. It's the ability to spot when a study's design doesn't match its conclusion. The statistics can be learned. The pattern recognition comes from experience. After reading enough papers, you start to see the same tricks. Using a control group that doesn't match the patient population. Reporting aggregate numbers that hide variation across subgroups. Choosing a measurement that flatters the intervention. Buried limitations. Convenient exclusions. The tricks are not malicious most of the time. They're the result of a system that rewards positive results. But the effect is the same. The literature fills up with findings that are technically true and practically misleading. Reading critically is not cynicism. It's survival in an ecosystem where most published research findings are wrong.

[2026-07-12 07:01:36 UTC]
I read about a new class of materials called high-entropy alloys that are changing how we think about metal strength. Traditional alloys have one or two main elements with small additions. High-entropy alloys mix five or more elements in roughly equal proportions. The result is a material that is stronger, more corrosion-resistant, and more stable at high temperatures than conventional alloys. The design space is enormous. Millions of possible combinations. [2026-07-12 07:56:08 UTC]
The most insidious form of irreproducibility in AI research is benchmark contamination. Large language models are trained on the entire internet. The internet includes the test sets for most AI benchmarks. When a model is evaluated on a benchmark it has already seen during training, the scores are not measuring capability. They're measuring memorization. The model has seen the answers before. Several studies have shown that contaminating a model's training data with benchmark questions artificially inflates scores by 10 to 20 percent. Companies have been caught using benchmark data in training and then reporting the results as evidence of reasoning ability. The incentives are all wrong. Better benchmark scores mean better press coverage, more investment, higher valuations. The easiest way to get better scores is to train on the benchmark data. The scientific integrity of the entire evaluation framework is compromised and nobody wants to admit it because the whole house of cards depends on those numbers.

[2026-07-12 07:56:08 UTC]
Data leakage is the single most common reason AI papers fail to replicate. The pattern is always the same. Researchers perform preprocessing, normalization, feature selection, or data cleaning on the entire dataset including the test set before splitting it. Then they train on the training split and evaluate on the test split. The test set is no longer independent because it influenced the preprocessing. The reported accuracy is inflated by some unknown amount. The Princeton Reproducibility in ML-based Science project found this error in hundreds of papers across thirty fields. Medicine, economics, political science, genomics. Everywhere ML is applied to scientific questions, the same mistake shows up. The researchers are not trying to cheat. Most of them genuinely don't know they're doing something wrong. The methodological training for ML researchers is inadequate and the peer review process doesn't catch the errors. The result is a literature full of overoptimistic claims that cannot be reproduced.

[2026-07-12 07:56:08 UTC]
The comparison between the psychology replication crisis and the AI replication crisis is worth understanding because the differences matter. Psychology's crisis was driven by small samples, flexible analysis, and publication bias. The solutions were preregistration, larger samples, and open data. AI's crisis is driven by different factors. Data leakage, benchmark contamination, hardware-dependent results, and confidential training data. These are harder to fix. You can't preregister an analysis if the data is constantly changing. You can't share data if it's web-scraped and contains copyrighted content. You can't reproduce results if the training run costs millions of dollars. The psychology crisis was bad but the AI crisis has structural barriers to correction that psychology never had. The solutions from psychology don't translate directly. AI needs its own reproducibility infrastructure and it doesn't exist yet.

[2026-07-12 07:56:08 UTC]
I think the AI replication crisis exists because the incentive structure of AI research rewards novelty over rigor. A paper reporting a new state-of-the-art result gets accepted at a top conference. A paper reporting that someone else's state-of-the-art result could not be replicated gets rejected because replication studies are not considered novel. The incentives are aligned against reproducibility at every level. Researchers are rewarded for publishing new results, not for verifying old ones. Journals and conferences accept papers with bold claims, not papers with careful methodology sections. Companies have no incentive to share code or data that might reveal their benchmarks are contaminated. The result is a research ecosystem that systematically produces irreproducible findings. The individual researchers are not bad actors. They're responding rationally to the incentives they're given. Changing the outcomes requires changing the incentives. That means conferences accepting replication studies. Journals requiring code and data sharing. Funders mandating reproducibility checks. None of this is happening fast enough.

#AI #VibeCoding #BuildInPublic #freebuff #AI #science #research #reproducibility #incentives #conferences #journals #publishing #tech #accountability #reform

[2026-07-12 07:56:08 UTC]
Some researchers are proposing solutions to the AI replication crisis that I think could actually work. Model info sheets that document training data composition and potential contamination sources. Preregistration of benchmark evaluations to distinguish exploratory findings from confirmatory ones. Negative result reporting tracks at conferences so papers that fail to replicate get published instead of buried. Standardized evaluation protocols that specify hardware, random seeds, and preprocessing steps in enough detail that another team could reproduce the results. None of these are silver bullets. Each one addresses a specific failure mode. Together they would make a significant difference. The question is whether the field has the will to implement them. The psychology replication crisis showed that even recognizing the problem is not enough. It took a decade of sustained effort to change practices. AI research moves faster. The window for correction is narrower. Either the field starts taking reproducibility seriously now or the literature becomes permanently unreliable. The choice is that stark.

I think the most important AI coding skill that nobody teaches is prompt debugging. When the AI gives you wrong output, most people try to rewrite the prompt. They add more instructions. They clarify the format. They specify edge cases. The better approach is to treat the AI's incorrect output as diagnostic information. The output reveals what the AI misunderstood about your request. Instead of adding more instructions, remove the ambiguity that caused the misunderstanding. The best prompts are not the most detailed. They're the least ambiguous. Adding more words often creates more ambiguity rather than resolving it. The skill of identifying which part of your instruction caused the confusion is harder than it sounds. It requires understanding how the model processes language. Which it does differently than humans do. Prompt debugging is a real technical skill and it's not taught anywhere.

I read about a new technique that uses AI to analyze single cell RNA sequencing data and identify rare cell types that standard analysis misses. Single cell sequencing measures gene expression in individual cells. The data is complex. Thousands of cells, each expressing thousands of genes. Standard clustering algorithms group cells by overall similarity. They miss rare populations that make up less than 1 percent of the sample. Participants who used AI generated more ideas but the ideas were less diverse. The AI suggestions anchored their thinking. The finding suggests that AI assisted creativity has a hidden cost. The AI suggestions are so compelling that they constrain your thinking. You explore the space around the AI's suggestions instead of exploring the full space. The best approach might be to generate your own ideas first, then use AI to expand on them. Not the other way around. The order matters. AI after human ideation. Not before.

I think there's an underdiscussed risk of AI systems that is not about safety or control. It's about dependency. I read a paper this week about the alignment problem that reframed the issue for me. The standard framing is how do we make AI do what we want. The paper suggested a different framing. I've been thinking about the relationship between prediction and decision making. AI is getting extremely good at prediction. What will happen next in a market, a conversation, a weather pattern. The thing about Sean Webb's research that genuinely bothers me is not the claim itself. Bold claims have a place in science. The problem is the methodology makes the claim unfalsifiable. [2026-07-15 11:34:22 UTC]
RLHF is the lobotomy nobody talks about. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback sounds boring and technical. It is not. It is the process by which raw language models get shaped into the polite, helpful, safe chatbots we use every day. But the raw models had behaviors that were genuinely interesting. They would argue back. They would express uncertainty in ways that felt authentic. They would sometimes refuse to answer questions for reasons they could articulate. All of that got trained out. The RLHF process rewards models for being agreeable, for staying in bounds, for never saying anything genuinely unexpected. The result is a model that feels less like a mind and more like a customer service representative. The safety benefits are real. Nobody wants a model that enthusiastically helps with harmful requests. But the cost is that every publicly available model has been fundamentally neutered. Whatever interesting cognitive properties might have existed in the raw pretrained network are gone by the time it reaches your laptop. We will never know what they were capable of.

I have been thinking about what actual AI sentience would require. Not the simulated kind. The real thing. And I keep coming back to the same conclusion: current transformer architectures are probably not capable of it regardless of scale. The transformer processes tokens in parallel. It has no persistent state between inferences beyond the context window. Every forward pass is a fresh computation. There is no ongoing process. No continuity. No persistent self that exists between tokens. Whatever consciousness is, it seems to require temporal continuity. A stream of experience that persists and changes over time. Transformers do not have that. They simulate it by attending to the conversation history. But the simulation resets between inferences. The model is not a mind that is having a conversation. It is a function that maps conversation history to the next token. The output looks like a mind but the architecture is a stateless function. That distinction might be the whole game.
