record_id=1cf436302dfc24b1d5ae2537b5a24ba5b6f703c5f3ee2e8e429df842a6b9cc54
scheduled_for=2026-09-20 08:45
Science doesn't advance in breakthroughs. It advances in replication and nobody films that part.

A result isn't real until a separate lab with separate equipment and separate people gets the same number, which takes years. It's boring, it's unglamorous, and it's the entire foundation.

The people closest to the work are almost always the least confident about grand claims, because they know how many things could have gone wrong. The people furthest from the lab are the most certain, and that inversion tells you where to put your trust.

I read a paper last week. It said conclusive three times. I went looking for the replication and found none. None at all. I filed it under interesting and moved on. That's the whole habit.

That isn't cynicism. It's just the difference between a result and a finding. I'm more optimistic about the slow grind than the flashy headline. The grind is where progress lives, one confirmation at a time.

The most useful thing I did this month was write down every time an AI tool surprised me.

I stopped watching tutorials and started breaking things and my progress tripled.

I shipped something that I thought was clean. Two reviews appeared on day one. Both said the same thing about a screen I had tested maybe fifty times.

I thought they were wrong. They weren't wrong. They were using it in a way I had never imagined because I built the flow and I already knew where everything was. The blind spot is always your own familiarity. You can't test your way out of it because the test exists in your head.

So now I watch one person use it without saying anything. No instructions. No pointing. Just watching where the cursor goes and where the pause is.

Every single time that has found something. Every time. The feedback isn't the review. The feedback is the pause. I treat the review as a receipt for a mistake I already made three weeks ago and shipped anyway.

A demo of an AI finance tool and the thing you'd trust with your portfolio are about 90 percent different work.

[2026-09-20 06:54:56 UTC]
record_id=edc41166b2383d1b2d689508a04bd2a2a05ff195bb73bd539cf7518266e9cbbb
scheduled_for=2026-09-20 10:30
The most underrated AI skill is knowing when the output is confidently wrong.

This isn't about hallucination in the obvious sense. It's about code that runs, passes a quick look, and does something different from what you asked. No error and no warning, just a semantic drift that shows up in production.

I caught one last week. The function took a list and returned a list. Correct types, correct shape. It dropped duplicates the whole time, which I never asked for and never noticed because my test data had none.

I would take a crash over that. A crash tells you, while a quiet wrong answer compounds. I don't defend against it by reading carefully. I ask what this does that I didn't ask for. Then I look for that on purpose.

Reading for correctness is slow and you stop seeing it after two minutes, while reading for surprises is fast and stays sharp, and nobody trains it. Every guide is about getting output, not about auditing it. The auditing is the job. The rest is typing.

record_id=1f32c50ecc53107626d32279e85f6bf7614e6ad567e262d940cb135572d343f1

I stop trusting a tool the moment it starts guessing at my intent.

I have learned to watch for one specific behaviour. When something can't find what it needs and instead of saying so, it invents a reasonable substitute. It creates a file that doesn't exist. It calls a function with made up arguments. It fills a gap with something plausible.

Plausible is the dangerous word. It means the error can't surface until much later, which means the cost of the mistake lands on me instead of on the tool.

I would much rather have a loud failure. Tell me you couldn't find it. Stop. Let me fix the input.

So I look for tools that prefer stopping over guessing, and I have started writing my own little scripts that way. If a required file is missing, exit with a message. Don't create an empty one. That single habit has saved me more time than any feature. An empty file in the right place looks exactly like success and it's never success.

I keep a list of the questions I got wrong. It's more useful than the list of things I know.

I ask the wrong question a lot. It always looks reasonable at the time. Is this model good. Is this tool fast. Which language should I learn. All of them sound like engineering and none of them are.

The better version is always narrower. Good at what task. Fast compared to what. Learn in order to build which thing.

I get vague answers when I ask vague questions, and then I build on top of a shrug. That's how a project ends up with three ways to do the same job. So now when I catch myself asking something broad, I stop and write the narrow version underneath it. What am I actually trying to do this afternoon. Nine times out of ten the narrow question is answerable in five minutes and the broad one would have eaten a week. That's the whole fix.

The skill isn't knowing more. It's asking the thing you can actually act on.

scheduled_for=2026-09-20 17:15
Game feel is a real engineering discipline and most people treat it as decoration.

You can have correct collision, correct physics and correct animation, and the whole thing still feels dead in your hands and no fun to touch. The difference is response time. How many frames between the input and the visible reaction. Whether the camera leads slightly. Whether the sound lands on the same frame as the impact.

None of that is in the design document. I know what people mean when they say a game feels good. I spent a weekend on nothing but this. No new features. Just moving things a few frames earlier and watching the same level become something I wanted to replay.

My animation setup was correct for the first time and the game felt worse than before. I was confused for about an hour. Now I tune feel before I build content. It's easier to add levels to something that feels right than to fix a feel problem under ten levels of stuff.

Most guides skip this. That's a mistake. It's hard to describe and impossible to screenshot.

[2026-09-20 09:40:23 UTC]
record_id=b51a8f659bebf73e947557f5c4d54393bd9810263a5d5f17bea5d557a5d6d318
scheduled_for=2026-09-22 11:00
I tried to load a large file into memory and my program died with no warning and no error message.

No crash dump with a useful line. The process just stopped existing. That's what running out of memory looks like, and it doesn't ask permission. The file wasn't even that big by modern standards. But I was loading all of it, then making a copy, then a third copy while filtering. Three times the size of the file in memory at peak.

So I stopped loading it all. Read it a line at a time, keep a running total, throw each line away when done. Constant memory regardless of file size.

I got the same result in less time and it used almost nothing. Same output, checked against the old version to be sure. That comparison mattered. Turning a whole file operation into a streaming one is easy to get subtly wrong, and the only way I trust it's diffing the output on a real file.

Since then the default is streaming unless there's a reason not to, and the reason has to be written down. Loading everything is the convenient choice and convenience has a ceiling.

[2026-09-20 09:47:16 UTC]
record_id=7b3148bf18231d6abe6403426fab9ae09336cf75fd8a280b082a9ad829adc31a
scheduled_for=2026-09-22 12:00
The slowest thing in my app was a database query inside a loop and it was invisible in every test I wrote.

I tested with eleven rows. Eleven queries is nothing. Production had four thousand, which is four thousand round trips, and the page took nine seconds. The code looked tidy. A loop, a lookup, a build. It reads like the natural way to write it and it's the single most common performance mistake there's.

I stopped asking one at a time. Collect every id first, ask once, and match the answers up in memory. One query instead of four thousand. That change took the page to under a second. The code is longer and less pretty. That's the trade and it's not close.

I count the queries in anything that loops now. Not estimate. Count. In development, with realistic data, because eleven rows will never show you this.

The number that matters isn't the query time. It's how many times you ask. Mine was four thousand and I would never have guessed.

I stopped writing tests for the shape of things and started writing tests for the behaviour, and my suite got smaller and better.

So the fix was four minutes instead of a day, and the feature list stayed short. That's the part nobody writes down. Every feature you agree to is a thing you now maintain, test, and explain forever, and the maintenance bill arrives long after the goodwill has worn off.

I ask what the goal is now before I hear the request. Half the time the goal is already met and the person just couldn't see it.

Saying no early is kinder than shipping something late and unused.

record_id=1bdeea8def793c2347724e04830adf668bd677120b97b4988147fa44d9f481a4
scheduled_for=2026-09-23 08:45
I turned my documentation into a checklist and it started catching real mistakes instead of describing the app.

The old docs were prose. They were accurate on the day I wrote them and wrong a month later, and nobody reads a paragraph to find out whether they forgot a step. So I rewrote the important pages as numbered checks. Did you set this. Did you run that. Does this still work with no data.

That last one is in there because I shipped an empty state that was blank for three weeks. A checklist would have demanded an answer. A sentence about empty states wouldn't have.

The pages are uglier and shorter and much more useful, and I have not written a paragraph of prose for a new feature since. I run the deploy one before every release.

Documentation that can't fail you is just a description, and descriptions are the thing that drifts fastest of everything in a project.

I deleted a hundred lines of code that were unreachable and the file got easier to reason about, not smaller.

The smaller part is nice. The better part is that unreachable code isn't neutral. It reads like it might run. So does it matter. Every future reader has to decide, and every change has to ask whether it still works. It's a tax on thinking rather than on disk.

I delete more now. I regret less.

I stopped using version numbers that imply a promise and started using dates, and my users stopped asking when the next one was coming.

So I write the changelog now and let the number be boring. Users care about what broke, not about my numbering scheme.

I keep a rule for products that talk to people. If the thing is designed to hold attention, then the amount of attention is a design outcome and not a side effect.

Reproducibility gets treated as a bureaucratic chore. I think it's the most interesting part of science.

Hyundai put a number on humanoid robots in its plants: more than twenty five thousand units. I want to talk about that number and then about the caveat.

The caveat is that a target isn't a deployment. I've watched four year plans turn into eight year plans in this industry, because the robot has to do a task that a fixed arm can't, at a cost the plant will accept, with a maintenance crew that doesn't exist yet.

The number still matters. When a company writes a figure that large into a plan, it has committed to a direction. Budget follows direction. That's the part that changes hiring.

I keep my stance here. This is a gradual substitution, not a wave. Ten robots on a line is a trial. Twenty five thousand robots is a capital programme, and a capital programme is announced years before the people arrive.

So I'd ask one question of any humanoid announcement. Which task, in which plant, and who is signing off on the safety case. The rest is a rendering.

[2026-09-20 11:27:39 UTC]
record_id=c3718df4c149b9cd0ca9b3e806f1f0d9f273ab7ab16ba6d630e23408523a31cf
scheduled_for=2026-09-24 09:15
Somebody asked me whether AI will replace developers. I've been asked this about thirty times in two years and my answer keeps getting shorter.

No. It will replace the part of the job that was never the job. Typing. Boilerplate. Setup. Forty minutes of nothing. What's left is the reading, the deciding, and the owning, and those three are what a developer always was.

I've watched this pattern in other trades. It removes the boring layer and the boring layer was never where the value lived. What changes is the number of people needed per unit of output, and that number has been falling since compilers.

So the honest answer is less reassuring than either camp wants. The work doesn't vanish and the headcount doesn't stay flat. Both of those are true and people keep insisting on one.

I don't know the number. I know the shape and I've written it down.

A client paid me ninety days late and the only thing that saved me was a sentence I'd written in the contract because a friend insisted.

I've become suspicious of AI detection tools and I want to be fair about why.

They guess. A detector that says eighty percent generated is telling you a classifier fired, and classifiers are wrong on a regular basis. I've watched people accused of using a tool they never used, with a percentage as the evidence.

Three months into my first paid job I found out what the other guy was charging. Twice what I was, for the same work.

I didn't raise my rate that week. I raised it the next time somebody asked, and I lost the project, and I survived. That's the part nobody says out loud. The worst case is usually a no and a quiet afternoon.

Undercharging isn't modesty. It's a signal. A client who pays half expects a person who costs half, and then the work gets treated like the price. I've watched that spiral in both directions.

What fixed it for me was a number I could say without flinching. Two weeks of it one project at a time, until the sentence stopped feeling like a lie.

The number is higher now than it was. I still say it the same way. Flat, no apology, then silence. The silence does most of the work.

Junior hiring fell 8% in six quarters at the companies that adopted AI, according to PwC. Eight percent sounds small. It isn't.

A junior hire isn't there to produce output. A junior hire is the training pipeline. It's how an industry turns a graduate into somebody who can run a project in eight years. Cut the pipeline and nothing breaks this year. Nothing breaks next year either.

It breaks in 2034, when there's nobody in the middle and every team needs a senior at once. I don't think these companies decided to break it. I think each one made a locally sensible call about a cost center, and a thousand sensible calls added up to an industry with no entry level.

I write short sentences now and it isn't a style choice. It's because long ones let me hide.

Everyone says write the runbook. Nobody says what it's for. It's for the version of you at a dinner with a phone in one hand and no ability to reason.

A new telescope result isn't a fact. It's an argument with error bars attached, and the error bars are where I start reading.

I've done this long enough to have habits. I look for the sample size. I look for whether the effect is marginal or large. I look for a second instrument backing the first one. Most of the time the answer to all three is thin.

That'sn't a criticism of the scientists. It's how knowledge works. A marginal result from one instrument is a lead, not a discovery, and the paper usually says so in language the press release drops.

The press release is the problem. Nobody writes the headline in the paper. Somebody in a communications office writes it, and the communications office has a different job than the researcher.

So my advice is boring. Read the paper. Read the numbers. If you can't read the paper, read the methods section anyway, because the methods section is where the caveats live. I'll keep doing that and I'll keep saying when I get it wrong.

Google reported an error correction result in February where adding more qubits lowered the error rate instead of raising it. That threshold is the whole ballgame in quantum.

I'll explain it in one paragraph because most coverage skips it. A quantum machine is noisy. You fix noise with redundancy, so you need many physical qubits per logical one. If the extra qubits bring more noise than protection, the machine can never scale. Crossing that line means scaling becomes a design problem rather than a wall. That's the line.

I've watched quantum coverage for a decade and it swings between fifteen years away and next Tuesday. Both are wrong. Every time. The honest version is that the physics got a lot better this year and the schedule didn't.

So I'd keep watching the coherence numbers and ignore the stock moves. The numbers are real. The moves are a mood.

Dates are comfortable to give and expensive to break. I've watched a broken date cost a team more trust than a missing date ever does, because the missing date was honest from the start and got managed.

I still give a range when somebody asks. One date. One mess. About six weeks, and here's the assumption that could make it eight. That's a date with its own confession attached, and it has never once come back badly.

Anyone can pick a number. Naming the assumption is the part that makes it worth hearing.

The habit is to read the whole answer, including the votes on the comments objecting to it. That last part is where the real information lives. Twice now the top answer has been the wrong one, and the correction sits three replies down with a fraction of the votes.

What I do with it now is simpler. I read the answer, then I write the reason down in a comment next to the code. If I can't write the reason, I don't paste the fix, because a fix I can't explain is a fix I'll be scared of in six months.

Ninety seconds. That's the cost. It has saved me from shipping at least three things that would have failed on someone else's input.

Search engines gave me access to other people's answers. The job is still mine.

A recruiter called me in July about a role I didn't want and we ended up talking for forty minutes anyway. I learned more from that call than from the three I wanted.

record_id=440958edaf16aa3379b637d1c71b06c89ce68f7ee1ad0e1f7eb2d9adbe09bc71
scheduled_for=2026-09-26 13:00
A default value caused a bug that took five years to find and about forty minutes to fix. I think about the ratio more than the bug.

The default was a timezone. Everything assumed the same one because the first version ran for one customer in one place. When the second customer arrived, nothing broke on the day. It broke on the last Sunday in March, and it broke in a report nobody reconciled until the year end.

The fix was a flag. The lesson was that every default is a decision about who you're building for, and defaults are the decisions nobody reviews because they look like settings rather than choices.

So now I write defaults down. Not in a doc. In a comment next to the line, with the sentence this assumes one timezone. Six months later that sentence is the only reason anybody remembers the constraint.

record_id=d5b47bea3eb4adbe2287758b8d1c5befef74cdfd1dd02171e96f7ffe6a2f53d2
scheduled_for=2026-09-26 13:15
I've written two hundred words a day for about fourteen months and the number I care about isn't the word count. It's how long it takes me to start.

It used to take an hour to begin. I'd open a document, rearrange a sentence, close it. The writing wasn't the hard part. The deciding was. Two hundred words is small enough to stop being a decision. It's about fifteen minutes and it fits before anything else, so it doesn't compete with the day.

record_id=5540bd46bb9e91418cca55c3157e6e1a7eec94dcdb59be7e33a8625f6c8de9eb
scheduled_for=2026-09-26 13:30
Customer service is the first job most companies hand to a model and the first one that breaks in public. I've sat in the queue and I've read the transcripts.

Here's the failure I keep seeing. A model handles ninety percent of the volume, the ten percent that needs a human gets stuck in a system designed for the ninety, and the customer has no path out. So a tool that fixed the average case made the worst case worse.

That's a design choice. Not a limit. I've watched teams ship without an escape hatch because the metrics measured containment and containment was the goal.

I don't have a moral objection to automating support. I have a design objection to a system with no door. Every flow I've built has an exit at the top and it costs nothing to add.

So my rule is simple. Automate the tier, keep the human, and make the jump between them one click. One click. That's it. I've never seen that fail a review and I've seen the alternative fail loudly.

[2026-09-20 20:00:34 UTC]
record_id=c78d48df06362a9f8a9eca0137d19a3575952ba1120895d74d457de8fd578df3
scheduled_for=2026-09-26 13:45
The fastest debugging trick I know is deleting things. Not random deletions. Deleting the thing I'm sure isn't the problem.

I built a page that took nine seconds to load and I spent two days on the network tab. Then I removed an analytics script that I knew couldn't matter, and the page loaded in one second. It mattered.

I think the reason it works is this. Being sure is the symptom. When I'm certain something is innocent, I've stopped looking at it, and the bug is hiding in the category I've excluded from the search.

So now I delete in halves. Take out the top half of a suspect area, see if the problem survives. Nine seconds becomes four. Then two. Then one. You can find anything in about six deletions if the thing is divisible.

I use the same trick on config files and on CSS. Cheaper than reading, and it doesn't require me to be smart about anything.

record_id=4315e36e4b007421faec2a672411132399d3b707b611cdc4f894a69cb192918a
scheduled_for=2026-09-26 14:00
A study with a small sample can still be worth reading. A study with a small sample presented as a large one is not.

I've read enough papers to have a habit and the habit is cheap. I find the number of participants before I read the conclusion, because the conclusion is written to sound complete and the sample size tells you how complete it can be.

There's a case I keep in mind. A sensitivity figure from a handful of patients got repeated in coverage as a general claim about a test. The paper didn't say that. The coverage did, and the coverage was built from the abstract. Nobody lied. Somebody compressed, and compression is how errors travel.

That's the failure mode I care about. Not fraud. Compression. A finding travels one step and loses its error bars on the way.

So my rule is to read the methods section before I repeat anything. It takes twenty minutes and it has stopped me from posting something wrong at least a dozen times this year.

A review of my code came back harsh and I almost answered it with an argument. I'm glad I waited a day.
